extractions.name: Example: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2x^2 y'' + 6 xy' + 2y = 0, \qquad x>0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form $y=x^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+6x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+6\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+2{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +2] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +2 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +2 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1) & =0 \\ 2(\lambda +1)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation has a double root $\lambda = -1.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={c}_{1}{x}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-1}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{x}+\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{1}\operatorname{ln} x={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}x\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
3{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-15t{y}^{′}+27y=0,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-15t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+27{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 3\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-15\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+27{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[3\lambda (\lambda -1)-15\lambda +27] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3\lambda (\lambda -1)-15\lambda +27 & =0 \\ 3{\lambda }^{2}-18\lambda +27 & =0 \\ 3({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9) & =0 \\ 3(\lambda -3)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =3.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{3}+{c}_{2}{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{6}\operatorname{ln} x.

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+19x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+81{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+19\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+81{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+19\lambda +81] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+19\lambda +81 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+18\lambda +81 & =0 \\ (\lambda +9)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-9.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-9}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-9}\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+10t{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+10t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+10\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+10\lambda +8] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+10\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-2.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-2}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-2}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+22t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+50{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+22\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+50{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+22\lambda +50] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+22\lambda +50 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+20\lambda +50 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +25) & =0 \\ 2(\lambda +5)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-5.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-5}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+15x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+15\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+49{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+15\lambda +49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+14\lambda +49 & =0 \\ (\lambda +7)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-7.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+13t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+13\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+13\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda +6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-6}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+3t{y}^{′}+y=0,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-1}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-9x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-9x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-9\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =5.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-15x{y}^{′}+64y=0,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.name: Example: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y =c_1 x^{10}+ c_2x ^{10}\ln x ,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
x^2 y'' - 19 xy' + 100y = 0, \quad y(1) = 0,\quad  y'(1)=1, \quad x>0.
$$
extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=0.$ Substituting $y(1)= 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0= c_1.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition $y'(1) = 1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10{c}_{1}{x}^{9}+{c}_{2}{x}^{9}+10{c}_{2}{x}^{9}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y'(1)=1$ and $c_1 = 0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 1 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x) = x ^{10}\ln x .
$$

extractions.name: Question 3
extractions.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$

extractions.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-6t{y}^{′}+8y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-6t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-6\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)-6\lambda +8] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)-6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +8 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4) & =0 \\ 2(\lambda -2)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =2.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2t{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}t+2{c}_{2}t\operatorname{ln} t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 3 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=3{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}x\operatorname{ln} x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=1.$ Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =1+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=x+3x\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=6.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4{c}_{1}{x}^{3}+{c}_{2}{x}^{3}+4{c}_{2}{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=6$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =4(2)+{c}_{2} \\ 6 & =8+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2{x}^{4}-2{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

extractions.name: Question 10
extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-7x{y}^{′}+16y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{4}+{c}_{2}{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln} x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-7x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=6,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln} x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-5{c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}-5{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-5(2)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =2{x}^{-5}+13{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & =\frac{2+13\operatorname{ln} x}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=2.$ Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-5{c}_{1}{x}^{-6}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}-5{c}_{2}{x}^{-6}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-5(2)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =2{x}^{-5}+13{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & =\frac{2+13\operatorname{ln} x}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.name: Question 3
extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-5}\operatorname{ln} x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+11x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-17t{y}^{′}+81y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{t}^{9}+{c}_{2}{t}^{9}\operatorname{ln} t,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-17t{y}^{′}+81y,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=0.$ Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =9{c}_{1}{t}^{8}+{c}_{2}{t}^{8}+9{c}_{2}{t}^{8}\operatorname{ln} t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =9{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 3 & =0+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =3{t}^{9}\operatorname{ln} t.\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=1.$ Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-7{c}_{1}{x}^{-8}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}-7{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}\operatorname{ln} x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-7(1)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={x}^{-7}+8{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & =\frac{1+8\operatorname{ln} x}{{x}^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.name: Question 8
extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln} x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-9x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-9\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =5.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{5}+{c}_{2}{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln} x.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=-2$ into the general solution gives

$$
-2={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=4.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5{x}^{4}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{4}+5{c}_{2}{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln} x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=4$ and ${c}_{1}=-2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 4 & =-10+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-2{x}^{5}+14{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & =2{x}^{5}(7\operatorname{ln} x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-9x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=4,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-11t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{6}+{c}_{2}{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6{c}_{1}{t}^{5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{5}+6{c}_{2}{t}^{5}\operatorname{ln} t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 0 & =24+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =4{t}^{6}-24{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln} t \\  & =4{t}^{6}(1-6\operatorname{ln} t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-11t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-11\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+36{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-11\lambda +36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -6)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =6.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{6}+{c}_{2}{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln} t.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
4={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6{c}_{1}{t}^{5}+{c}_{2}{t}^{5}+6{c}_{2}{t}^{5}\operatorname{ln} t\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 0 & =24+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =4{t}^{6}-24{t}^{6}\operatorname{ln} t \\  & =4{t}^{6}(1-6\operatorname{ln} t).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+9t{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,y(1)=3,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+9t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+16{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+9\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+16{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+9\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+9\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-4.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-4}+{c}_{2}{t}^{-4}\operatorname{ln} t=\frac{{c}_{1}}{{t}^{4}}+\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} t}{{t}^{4}}.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=3$ into the general solution gives

$$
3={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\frac{4{c}_{1}}{{t}^{5}}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{t}^{5}}-\frac{4{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} (t)}{{t}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=3$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 3 & =-12+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=\frac{3+15\operatorname{ln} t}{{t}^{8}}.
$$

extractions.problem:
Find the solution of the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+3x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(2)=0,\,{y}^{′}(2)=1,\,x>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
The given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+3x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have a double root $\lambda =-1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-1}\operatorname{ln} x=\frac{{c}_{1}}{x}+\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} x}{x}.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(2)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2}{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{1}=-{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(2)=1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\frac{{c}_{1}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} (x)}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(2)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=-{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{{c}_{1}}{4}+\frac{{c}_{2}}{4}-\frac{{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2}{4} \\ 4 & =-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2 \\ 4 & ={c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2+{c}_{2}-{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2 \\ 4 & ={c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
{c}_{1}=-{c}_{2}\operatorname{ln} 2=-4\operatorname{ln} 2.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =-\frac{4\operatorname{ln} 2}{x}+\frac{4\operatorname{ln} x}{x} \\  & =\frac{4}{x}(\operatorname{ln} x-\operatorname{ln} 2) \\  & =\frac{4}{x}\,\operatorname{ln} (\frac{x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

extractions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-5t{y}^{′}+9y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{t}^{3}+{c}_{2}{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln} t,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-5t{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=5,\,t>0.
$$

extractions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=1.$ Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=5.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3{c}_{1}{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}{t}^{2}+3{c}_{2}{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln} t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=5$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5 & =3+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={t}^{3}+2{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln} t.\end{aligned}
$$
